title: Private landlords supply the large majority of Australia's rental housing
oneLiner: Social and institutional housing is a small share; most renters rent from an individual.
body: Census tenure data shows that most rented dwellings are owned by private individuals rather than by governments, community housing providers or institutional investors. Any policy that changes individual investors' behaviour therefore acts on most of the rental stock.
contextBackground: Australia's rental market is unusual in how little of it is institutional. This shapes every argument about investor incentives: there is no large alternative landlord class to absorb a change in individual investors' behaviour.
contextDisagreement: Not disputed as a fact. The disagreement is about what follows: whether reliance on individual landlords is a reason to protect their incentives, or a structural weakness to be addressed directly.

evidenceItems.citation: Australian Bureau of Statistics, Census of Population and Housing — tenure and landlord type

otherClaim.title: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market

claimItself.title: Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market
claimItself.oneLiner: Fewer landlords means fewer rentals, and fewer rentals means higher rents.
claimItself.body: If the after-tax return on rental property falls, some investors will sell and fewer will buy. Opponents of reform argue that the resulting withdrawal of rental stock would raise rents for the tenants the policy is meant to help.

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: Treasury estimates the 2026 changes would raise rents by less than $2 a week for a household on the median rent

ownArguments.label: FOR
ownArguments.text: Modelling commissioned by the property industry forecasts rents about $9 a week higher and roughly 8,700 fewer homes by 2030 under the changes

ownArguments.label: AGAINST
ownArguments.text: When negative gearing was quarantined in 1985–87, rents rose sharply in Sydney and Perth but not in other capitals

usedIn.relationSentence: This claim supports “Winding back negative gearing would push rents up as investors leave the market”

strengthDefinitions.decisive: The parent claim largely stands or falls on this one.
strengthDefinitions.relevant: It adds real weight, but the parent claim survives without it.
strengthDefinitions.tangential: True perhaps, but it does little work for this claim.
